column2: ST elevation in II, III, aVF with reciprocal depression in aVL is acute inferior STEMI. Pericarditis gives widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression.
Claudication (ABPI 0.6): stop smoking, statin, antiplatelet and supervised exercise; add cilostazol or naftidrofuryl if needed. Revascularise only if lifestyle-limiting or critical.
Anterior STEMI within 1 h: aspirin, potent P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor/prasugrel), anticoagulation and immediate primary PCI.
In ACS, glucose > 11 mmol/L is treated with a dose-adjusted IV insulin infusion (NICE CG130). Stop metformin around angiography and sulfonylureas acutely.
Chest pain with bradycardia and hypotension suggests inferior/RV MI; the RCA supplies the AV node and RV. Nodal block here is usually transient and atropine-responsive.
ST elevation in I and aVL is a high lateral infarct (circumflex or first diagonal). Anteroseptal = V1–V4; inferior = II, III, aVF.
NICE: CT coronary angiography is first line for suspected angina; functional imaging if non-diagnostic. Exercise ECG is no longer used for diagnosis.
Troponin stays raised 7–14 days, so for reinfarction at day 4 CK-MB (normal by 2–3 days) is more useful; a new hs-troponin rise > 20% is also used.
Bicuspid aortic valve has an associated aortopathy and raises dissection risk. Others: hypertension (commonest), Marfan, Loeys–Dietz, coarctation, Turner, pregnancy, cocaine.
CT angiography of the whole aorta confirms dissection in a stable patient; TOE if unstable. Chest X-ray and transthoracic echo cannot exclude it.
Type A dissection (ascending aorta) kills 1–2%/hour untreated: emergency surgery after IV beta-blocker BP/HR control. Type B is usually medical.
Proximal dissection can rupture into the pericardium causing tamponade, a leading cause of death; also acute AR, coronary occlusion and branch ischaemia.
Sudden severe chest pain in a hypertensive with no MI on ECG/troponin: exclude aortic dissection before antithrombotics or thrombolysis, which could be fatal.
An early diastolic murmur is aortic regurgitation; in Marfan syndrome aortic root dilatation stretches the valve ring. MVP gives a click and late systolic murmur.
Diabetes is consistently linked to fewer and slower-growing AAAs. Smoking is the strongest risk factor; also male sex, age, family history and hypertension.
Stopping smoking slows AAA growth and lowers rupture risk; drugs (ACEi, beta-blocker, statin) have not been shown to slow growth.
Pregnancy (third trimester/peripartum) predisposes to dissection through medial hormonal change and high cardiac output; this woman had no Marfan features.
Marfan syndrome is autosomal dominant, due to FBN1 (fibrillin-1) mutations: tall, ectopia lentis, aortic root dilatation and MVP. Sarcomere genes cause HCM.
A pseudoaneurysm is a contained rupture held only by adventitia or surrounding tissue (after puncture, surgery, trauma). A true aneurysm involves all three layers.
Degenerative aortic aneurysms are several times commoner in men, so female sex is not a risk factor. Age, smoking, hypertension and family history are.
Aortic root aneurysm with hypertelorism, bifid uvula and familial sudden death is Loeys–Dietz (TGFBR1/2); aneurysms dissect smaller, so repair earlier than Marfan.
Uncomplicated type B dissection (beyond the left subclavian) is treated medically with IV beta-blockade. Malperfusion, rupture or expansion need repair; any ascending involvement needs surgery.
Ascending aortic dilatation: GCA, Takayasu, syphilis, spondyloarthritis, Marfan/Loeys–Dietz/EDS, bicuspid valve. SLE is not a recognised cause.
A 3.0–3.5 cm AAA is monitored with ultrasound while treating risk factors; repair at ≥ 5.5 cm, growth > 1 cm/year or symptoms. EVAR is an alternative to open repair.
Tearing back pain, severe hypertension, new AR and widened mediastinum is proximal dissection: IV beta-blocker, then nitroprusside, urgent TOE/CT and surgery.
One-off ultrasound AAA screening is offered to men 65–75 who have ever smoked (all men at 65 in the UK); it reduces aneurysm deaths.
A young woman with prior systemic illness, chest pain and an absent radial pulse has Takayasu arteritis (large-vessel vasculitis); diagnose by CT/MR angiography, treat with steroids.
After ACS with a drug-eluting stent, DAPT continues ~12 months; stopping clopidogrel at 3 weeks risks fatal stent thrombosis. Defer elective surgery (≥ 6, ideally 12 months).
Coronary disease is the commonest cause of HFrEF; about half of heart failure is HFpEF, and 1-year mortality is still ~10–30%.
Orthopnoea, pink frothy sputum, crackles, raised JVP, oedema and cardiomegaly is acute decompensated heart failure. COPD/asthma give wheeze without a raised JVP.
Congestion in acute heart failure is treated with an IV loop diuretic (furosemide), sitting up, oxygen if hypoxic and nitrates if BP allows. Diltiazem is negatively inotropic.
Heart failure causes arrhythmias, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia (ACEi/MRA) and raised urea (cardiorenal). Hyperlipidaemia is a cause of the underlying CAD, not a complication.
Echocardiography is key: EF (HFrEF/HFmrEF/HFpEF), valves, wall motion, pericardium and filling pressures. Angiography comes later if ischaemia is suspected.
Spironolactone (MRA) improves symptoms and survival in HFrEF (RALES). Flecainide raises mortality in structural heart disease; NSAIDs worsen fluid retention.
If ACEi/ARB/ARNI cannot be used (renal impairment, hyperkalaemia), hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate reduces HFrEF mortality and does not raise potassium.
In HFpEF, SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) reduce heart-failure hospitalisation and CV death; diuretics for congestion and treat comorbidities.
Peripartum cardiomyopathy during pregnancy: beta-blocker and loop diuretic (hydralazine/nitrate if needed). ACEi, ARB, ARNI and MRA are unsafe before delivery.
ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta-blockers, MRAs and SGLT2 inhibitors reduce HFrEF mortality. Digoxin reduced admissions but not mortality (DIG trial).
In older patients with dilated cardiomyopathy, exclude coronary disease before calling it non-ischaemic, as revascularisation may help.
A heart-failure patient on only furosemide and aspirin lacks prognostic therapy: start an ACE inhibitor (also treats her BP), then beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2i.
Biventricular failure with cardiomegaly and global hypokinesia (EF 25–30%) in a young woman is dilated cardiomyopathy. Restrictive disease keeps systolic function.
ACE inhibitors (or ARB/ARNI) reduce HFrEF mortality and remodelling and are a cornerstone with beta-blockers, MRAs and SGLT2i. Non-DHP CCBs worsen HFrEF.
Evidence-based beta-blockers (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate) cut HFrEF mortality by ~a third; start low when euvolaemic and titrate slowly.
Loop diuretics relieve congestion and symptoms but do not improve survival; use the lowest dose that keeps the patient euvolaemic.
DCM predisposes to AF and ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden death is common; consider an ICD if EF stays ≤ 35% despite optimal therapy.
